summaries.example: Imagine saying, “The garden is wet.” It might be true now, but after the sun comes out it may be false. Prior wanted logic to talk about these changes. He used special signs for ideas such as “this will be true later” and “this was true earlier.”
summaries.summary: Arthur Prior was a philosopher and logician who invented tense logic. This is a way of using logical tools to talk about time. For example, a statement can be true now, have been true before, or become true later. Prior added special operators for future and past ideas and later built fuller systems connecting them. He also studied modal logic, which concerns possibility and necessity, and helped develop an early form of possible-worlds reasoning. Prior believed that formal logic should help us understand the world, including time, choice, obligation, and action. His work supported philosophical discussions about an open future and free will. Later, tense logic became useful in linguistics and computer science, where it can describe and check events that happen in sequence.
key_ideas: Arthur Prior created and developed tense logic, which helps us reason about past and future statements.
He thought logic should connect with the real world, not be only a game with symbols.
Prior used ideas about time to discuss whether the future is open and whether people can make choices.
His work later helped fields such as computing, including checking how programs behave over time.
He also helped develop ideas about possible worlds and how one possibility may be connected to another.
summaries.why_it_matters: Prior showed that logic can be used to study changing situations, not just unchanging facts. His ideas give people tools for discussing time, choices, and possibilities carefully. They also became useful for describing computer programs and checking whether events happen in the right order. His work is a reminder that difficult symbols can help us ask important questions about everyday life.

important_terms.definition: A careful system for checking whether statements fit together and whether a conclusion follows from reasons.
A kind of logic that studies how statements change when we think about earlier, present, or later times.
A word or sign that changes a statement into one about time, possibility, knowledge, duty, or another related idea.
The idea that some future events are not settled yet and may happen in more than one way.
A system that uses three choices for a statement: true, false, or not settled yet.

questions_to_think_about: Can a statement be true at one time and false at another time?
Is the future already fixed, or can choices help shape it?
Why might computers need a way to reason about what happens next?
Should logic be about real things as well as symbols?

summaries.example: Let p mean “the server is working.” A future operator can form Fp, read as “p will be true at some later time,” while a past operator can form Pp, read as “p was true at some earlier time.” If a system models a program, these operators can express claims such as “the program will eventually finish” or “the warning has already appeared.” The philosophical question is whether every future fact is already determined. Prior’s branching-time approach represents several possible continuations from the present rather than one unavoidable future.
summaries.summary: Arthur Prior’s most important achievement was the invention and development of tense logic, a formal study of propositions whose truth may vary with time. He introduced operators for future and past claims and developed systems in which futurity and pastness interact. Prior connected these systems with relations ordering dates, but he warned that such a relational calculus should not automatically be treated as the metaphysical meaning of tense: the indexical character of “now” is not captured simply by a date variable. His work was closely tied to the problem of future contingents and the Master Argument, an ancient argument associated with a deterministic conception of possibility. Prior used a three-valued approach to argue that some claims about undetermined future events can be indeterminate rather than simply true or false. He also defended a branching conception of time and used tense logic to make conceptual room for free will and indeterminism. Beyond tense, Prior contributed to general intensional logic, the study of modal concepts that are not merely about necessity and possibility. With Carew Meredith, he developed an early possible-worlds semantics involving an accessibility relation. The entry presents Prior as a logician who combined formal construction with historical and metaphysical questions. His systems later influenced work in linguistics and computer science, especially the description and verification of time-dependent and concurrent processes.
key_ideas: Prior treated tense as a form of modality and introduced operators for future and past claims.
His full tense calculi combined separate past and future systems with axioms describing how they interact.
Some principles in a tense calculus are logical, while others represent assumptions about time, such as transitivity, density, or the absence of a first or last moment.
Prior argued that a tenseless logic cannot fully express the difference between a fixed past and an open future.
His analysis of future contingents used three-valued logic to challenge a deterministic reading of the ancient Master Argument.
Prior and Carew Meredith developed an early possible-worlds framework using a relation between states, while later work by Kripke and others helped establish modern semantics.
summaries.why_it_matters: Prior’s work links technical logic with questions about reality: what it means for something to have happened, what may happen, and whether the future is settled. Temporal logic now supports formal reasoning about programs and systems whose states change over time. Philosophically, his work shows why the choice between a single linear future and branching possibilities affects how we understand truth, agency, and responsibility. His broader project also helped restore attention to the idea that formal systems should illuminate meaningful subject matter rather than be studied only as symbol manipulation.

important_terms.definition: A branch of modal logic that represents claims about what has been, is, or will be the case.
A formal expression that operates on a proposition, producing a claim about necessity, possibility, time, knowledge, obligation, or another mode.
A type of modality concerned with necessity and possibility, rather than with time, duty, or knowledge.
A view that future events, at least in some cases, are not already fixed by the present and past.
A formal system in which a proposition may receive true, false, or indeterminate status.
A representation of possible situations as points connected by a relation showing which situations are accessible from which others.
A relation in which one point or world is treated as reachable from another for purposes of interpreting modal claims.
A theory that treats the present as fundamental and understands past and future in relation to it.

questions_to_think_about: Does a statement about an unsettled future need to be either true or false now?
Which temporal principles are logical necessities, and which are claims about how time is physically structured?
Can a branching model represent freedom without proving that humans possess free will?
Should possible worlds explain modal operators, or should modal operators be treated as more basic?
How does temporal logic differ from ordinary propositional logic?

summaries.example: Suppose your class is deciding whether to hold a picnic tomorrow. The statement “the picnic will be outdoors” is about the future. Before the decision, several outcomes may still be possible: sunny weather, rain, or a change of plan. Prior’s tense logic gives us a careful way to mark claims about what will happen, what happened earlier, and what is always the case. A branching picture of time can show different possible paths from today.
summaries.summary: Arthur Prior was a pioneering philosopher and logician best known for creating tense logic. Tense logic uses formal operators to represent claims such as “it will be the case that p” and “it has been the case that p.” Prior developed increasingly rich systems joining future and past operators, and he examined which principles follow from logic alone and which depend on assumptions about time. For example, a rule may depend on time being transitive or dense, while another may follow from ordinary logical reasoning. Prior’s interest in tense was connected to the ancient problem of future contingents and the Master Argument. He rejected the idea that the argument automatically proves that everything is determined. Drawing on three-valued logic, he allowed that some claims about undetermined future events may be indeterminate. This supported his philosophical interest in an open, branching future and in free will. Prior also helped pioneer general intensional logic, extending modal methods to areas such as time, obligation, knowledge, and agency. His work with Carew Meredith contributed important early elements of possible-worlds semantics, including accessibility between possible situations. Although Prior worked with intricate formal calculi, he insisted that their value lay in what they could help us understand. Tense logic later became important in the study of natural language and in computing, where it can describe and verify changing states and concurrent activity.
key_ideas: Prior made tense logic a major area of formal study by adapting modal-logical methods to time.
He treated past and future as related but distinct, rather than simply adding dates to otherwise timeless statements.
His systems can include assumptions about time, such as whether it is continuous, ordered, branching, or has a first or last moment.
Prior used logic to examine the disagreement between determinism and indeterminism, especially concerning future events.
He believed formal logic should have a subject matter and should help clarify philosophical problems.
His ideas influenced later research in modal logic, linguistics, and computer science.
summaries.why_it_matters: Prior’s achievement was not only inventing new symbols. He showed how formal systems can make disagreements about time and possibility more exact. His distinction between logical principles and assumptions about the structure of time helps readers see what an argument really depends on. The later use of temporal logic in software verification demonstrates the practical reach of questions that began as investigations into ancient arguments about the future.

important_terms.definition: A formal system for reasoning about statements involving the past, present, and future.
A symbol or phrase that turns a statement into one about a mode such as possibility, necessity, pastness, or futurity.
The view that at least some future events are not fixed in advance and can develop in different ways.
A logic that allows a statement to be true, false, or neither settled as true nor false.
A way of explaining possibility by considering different possible situations or worlds.
A relation indicating which possible situations can be considered reachable from another situation.
A traditional argument claiming that what is neither true now nor going to be true cannot be genuinely possible.

questions_to_think_about: If a future event is not settled, should its statement be called false, or is a third status needed?
What is gained by representing time as a branching tree instead of a single line?
Can a formal system describe freedom without settling the larger metaphysical debate about free will?
Why might a computer scientist care whether an event happens eventually or always?
What should be more basic: statements about tense, or a relation ordering times?
